description: Walk the royal-palm-lined boulevard running from Government House down to the waterfront and you're on the most iconic public space in Port Louis - and its own open-air history lesson. name: Aapravasi Ghat World Heritage Site
description: You're standing at the place where the modern indentured-labour diaspora began - though the practice itself predates this exact building. The first 36 indentured labourers reached Mauritius on 2 November 1834 aboard the ship Atlas, which had left India that September; they landed near the old Customs House, just metres from where you're standing now, fifteen years before this purpose-built depot even existed. Built in 1849, the Aapravasi Ghat - literally the 'Immigration Depot' - became the main entry point for almost 500,000 indentured labourers brought to Mauritius between 1849 and 1923, mostly from India but also China, Africa, Madagascar and Southeast Asia, to work the island's sugar plantations after the abolition of slavery. New arrivals bathed after weeks at sea, were medically inspected and vaccinated against smallpox, had their contracts read aloud in their own language, and usually spent about two days here completing the paperwork before being sent out to sugar estates across the island. It's been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006.
interesting_fact_1: Roughly 70% of Mauritians today are descended from these indentured labourers - making this small 1,640 m² depot one of the most significant sites anywhere for understanding the roots of modern Mauritian society, and one of the earliest examples of a labour-migration system that would go on to reshape economies worldwide.

name: Line Barracks
address: Line Barracks St, Port Louis, Mauritius
description: In the heart of Port Louis stands a former colonial military barracks - inaugurated in 1740, making it almost as old as Government House itself - later repurposed as a police headquarters and formally listed by the Mauritius National Heritage Fund as a Scheduled Ancient Site. Barracks like this once housed the garrisons that controlled the island under both French and British rule, and the buildings' long institutional afterlife as a police compound has helped keep much of the original colonial-era structure intact. It's also been the operational nerve centre for some of the city's worst unrest in living memory - the 1967 election riots, the 1968 pre-independence riots, and the 1999 riots that followed the death in police custody of Kaya, the country's most famous seggae musician, were all commanded and coordinated from here.
interesting_fact_1: Line Barracks still functions as an operational police headquarters today, making it a rare case of a Port Louis heritage site that has never stopped being used for the purpose it was originally built for - military and civil order - across more than two centuries.

name: Trou Fanfaron
description: This stretch of Port Louis harbour is where, from 1849, ships carrying indentured labourers from India actually docked and unloaded their passengers before they were processed at the neighbouring Aapravasi Ghat depot - clerks chalked numbers onto new arrivals' coats and doctors inspected them for scurvy and smallpox right here on the wharf, vaccinating anyone who hadn't already been, before the first labourers were marched off within days to sugar estates across the island. Anyone suspected of carrying a contagious disease never made it this far - they were quarantined instead, often on remote islets off the coast, a precaution that failed catastrophically in 1856 when around 300 Indian arrivals died of cholera in the rudimentary quarantine camp on Gabriel Island, 12km offshore.
interesting_fact_1: By 1860 the facility here had been expanded to process up to 600 immigrants at a time - a scale that gives some sense of just how relentless the flow of new arrivals through this one stretch of wharf really was.

name: Bourbon Street Food Vendors
address: Bourbon Street, near Central Market, Port Louis, Mauritius
description: Walk this stretch of Bourbon Street, right by Port Louis Central Market, and you'll find some of the best-loved everyday Mauritian street food sold each morning - dholl puri (soft split-pea flatbreads filled with spiced bean curry and rougaille sauce), crunchy gateaux piments (chilli-lentil fritters) and fresh alouda drinks, dished out from stalls locals queue for on their way to work.
interesting_fact_1: Dholl puri is so central to Mauritian daily life it's often called the island's unofficial national dish, despite being sold almost exclusively from unglamorous street stalls rather than restaurants - weekday mornings from around 7 to 10:30am are peak time to catch it fresh. The dish was invented essentially by accident: plantation labourers' wives, making the most of what they had, kneaded their flour dough with the same water dal had just been boiled in, and leftover lentil grains ended up baked right into the bread. But it wasn't sold on street corners until after independence in 1968 - the widespread poverty of that era created the market for something this filling, cheap and portable, and it's been a fixture of Mauritian street food ever since.

name: Jim Boulettes
description: This no-frills stall on Bourbon Street is famous among Port Louis regulars for boulettes - small Chinese-Mauritian steamed or fried dumplings, sold cheap and fast, that count among the island's most popular grab-and-go snacks.
interesting_fact_1: Boulettes reflect Mauritius's 19th-century Chinese immigration just as directly as the pagodas and Chinatown gate elsewhere on this tour - descended from Cantonese dim sum traditions, they've become so thoroughly adopted into everyday Mauritian eating habits that most people no longer think of them as "Chinese food" at all. The dish itself changed to fit the island: traditional Hakka boulettes used cabbage, but Cantonese-Mauritian cooks swapped in chayote (christophine) since cabbage wasn't always available locally - a small substitution that's now just how it's made.
